name: Rudolf Hess
role: Deputy Führer of the Nazi Party (1933–1941); Reichsminister without portfolio (1933–1941)
summary: Rudolf Hess was Hitler's Deputy Führer and a close confidant until 1941. He argued for a single leader with unrestricted power against parliamentary majorities, backed the Nazi party's rule, the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and the annexations of Austria, the Sudetenland and Poland, and called for the destruction of Marxist and Bolshevik organizations. In May 1941 he flew to Scotland carrying peace terms, and he was later convicted at Nuremberg on the counts of crimes against peace and conspiracy.

sources.title: The Oath to Adolf Hitler (speech, 25 February 1934)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Broadcast oath speech: loyalty and absolute obedience to Hitler, leaders as examples, Hitler sent by higher powers, reason versus heart, service to the whole, Hitler Youth discipline

sources.title: Electing Adolf Hitler Führer (speech, August 1934)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Pre-referendum speech: argument for one leader with unrestricted power against parliament and separation of powers, providence, Roman dictatorship, plebiscite, Hitler's rise and the 1934 yes-vote appeal

sources.title: The Launching of the Training Ship Horst Wessel (speech, 1935)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Speech on naming a training ship: Horst Wessel as martyr, instilling loyalty to the Führer and to Germany in young men

sources.title: To the Front Fighters of the World (speech, 8 July 1934)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Speech on peace and armaments: front-soldier camaraderie, peace with France and Poland, limited German armaments, trade and peace, rejection of parliamentary majorities as representing interest groups

sources.title: From Revolution to Construction (speech, Gau Essen rally, 25 June 1934)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Speech on party unity: one movement instead of thirty parties, action against critics and saboteurs, Marxist organizations destroyed, Bolshevism and the 1934 'second revolution' dismissed, revolution directed by Hitler, rearmament of the economy and family and racial policy

sources.title: Reich Citizenship Law and Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor (15 September 1935)
sources.author: Reichstag (laws promulgated at Nuremberg; text as translated by USHMM)
sources.usedFor: Text of the two Nuremberg Laws, which bear Hess's signature as Deputy of the Führer on the Blood Law

sources.title: Judgment: Hess (Nuremberg International Military Tribunal)
sources.author: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg
sources.usedFor: Tribunal's findings on Hess: supported rearmament and the 1935 conscription law, role in the Austria, Sudetenland and Poland annexations and decrees, the 1941 flight, and that proposed anti-Jewish laws were not sufficiently linked to war crimes

sources.title: Trial of the Major War Criminals, session of 31 August 1946 (Hess's final statement)
sources.author: Rudolf Hess
sources.usedFor: Hess's final statement at Nuremberg: refusal to defend himself against accusers, the Führer as his lifetime leader, no regrets, foreign-policy aims and armament, the 1923 revolution and atrocities, and his own religious belief

sources.title: Nuremberg trial transcript, prosecution case against Hess (7 February 1946)
sources.author: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg (Harvard Law School Nuremberg Trials Project)
sources.usedFor: Prosecution quotations of a 28 August 1938 Hess speech to the Foreign Organization (Volksdeutsche, Sudeten Germans, Poland) and of the British record of Hess's May 1941 interview with the Duke of Hamilton, which gives his peace terms

sources.title: Rudolf Hess
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Overview: Deputy Führer post, Volksdeutscher Rat, role of his office in the Nuremberg Laws, the 1941 flight and its aftermath, Spandau imprisonment, and secondhand reports of speeches (not verified against the speech texts)

notes: Hess's record is mostly speeches of 1933-1938 and the decrees and laws he signed. Signed laws are treated as measures only where the tribunal or his office's drafting role is recorded; a signature alone is not a stated view. His 1941 peace terms are known from a British record of his interview with the Duke of Hamilton (cited via the Nuremberg transcript), not from his own words. Later accounts (Spandau, Speer) are secondhand. His claim at Nuremberg of amnesia is recorded by Wikipedia as possibly a ruse. Several speech quotations about Jews and the League of Nations come from Wikipedia and could not be checked against the speech texts, so they are low.
